title: Beyond Bollywood: How Abhishek Bachchan Quietly Built a Second Career in Sports
excerpt: From kabaddi to football to European cricket, the actor has assembled a growing portfolio of sports franchises that he now calls a 'second profession.'
body:
• Abhishek Bachchan owns the Jaipur Pink Panthers in the Pro Kabaddi League (champions in 2014 and 2022), co-owns Chennaiyin FC in the Indian Super League (two-time ISL winners), and is co-owner of the European T20 Premier League.
  • He and his father Amitabh Bachchan also invested in the Majhi Mumbai franchise in the Indian Street Premier League, a T10 tennis-ball cricket tournament.
  • Bachchan started with kabaddi and football in 2014 while his Bollywood peers went straight to the IPL, deliberately choosing sports where he felt he could make a difference.
  • He describes sports ownership as having evolved from an "expensive hobby" into a "second profession" that he can now macro-manage as a self-sustaining business.

The Kabaddi Bet

While Shah Rukh Khan, Preity Zinta and Juhi Chawla were buying into the Indian Premier League in 2008, Abhishek Bachchan took a different path. He waited six years. And when he finally put money into sports in 2014, he chose kabaddi — a sport most people still associated with rural playgrounds and mud.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=bDfKcoVddX4

The decision was instinctive. When commentator Charu Sharma, who co-founded Mashal Sports with Anand Mahindra, first approached Bachchan about kabaddi at a social event, the actor was skeptical. Then he went to watch a few matches in the suburbs of Mumbai.

"At certain venues, there were close to 8,000-10,000 people watching and cheering the players. That's when I decided that I had to be a part of this."

— Abhishek Bachchan, Forbes India

He bought the Jaipur Pink Panthers, which won the inaugural Pro Kabaddi League championship that same year. The team won again in 2022. More importantly for Bachchan the businessman, kabaddi became profitable for him by the second season in 2015.

The stakes were personal. He was the only non-corporate owner in the league. "The rest were huge corporates," he told Forbes India. "For corporates, the cost of running a team was perhaps equivalent to their monthly advertising budget, but for me, it meant signing three films to bankroll it."

Football and the Long Game

Later in 2014, Bachchan also co-acquired Chennaiyin FC in the Indian Super League. The football team won the ISL title twice, but unlike kabaddi, football has been a slower burn financially.

https://x.com/dna/status/2090136819291828450

Bachchan is unfazed. "Football might not have the meteoric rise like kabaddi, but India will become a formidable football-playing nation," he has said. He points to the fact that some of the world's oldest football clubs have been around for more than a century. Patience, he argues, is part of the sport.

The Cricket Leap

For years, Bachchan deliberately avoided cricket — not because he lacked interest, but because he was not sure what he could bring to a sport already dominated by established franchise owners.

That changed when he and his father Amitabh Bachchan invested in Majhi Mumbai, a franchise in the Indian Street Premier League, a T10 tennis-ball cricket league. Bachchan described it as a "litmus test" — a way to get his feet wet in cricket before committing to something bigger.

The bigger move came when he became co-owner of the European T20 Premier League, an ICC-sanctioned franchise tournament in partnership with Ireland, Scotland and the Netherlands. The first season featured six teams from Dublin, Belfast, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Edinburgh and Glasgow.

"It's become a second profession, and I'm enjoying it. I have the belief that I can turn it into a business and set up a well-oiled machinery that can take care of itself — something I don't need to micromanage."

— Abhishek Bachchan, CNBC TV-18

A Differentiated Strategy

Marketing experts say Bachchan's approach stands apart from Bollywood's typical sports investments. "Backing kabaddi stands out as a differentiation vis-a-vis Bollywood's fixation with cricket," branding consultant Harish Bijoor told Forbes India. "His spirit of a thinking investor and an entrepreneur betting on his gut feel and passion makes him stand out."

Bachchan himself frames it in terms of impact rather than returns. He chose to co-own a league rather than buy into the IPL because he wanted to take cricket to markets that do not already have it. "Here was an opportunity to bring T20 entertainment to Europe, to a market which doesn't have that already," he told Storyboard18.

What's Next

Asked whether an IPL team is on the horizon, Bachchan is cautious. "I think the IPL has set the standard for how teams should be run. I want some more time before I can do that." For now, his portfolio — kabaddi, football, street cricket and European T20 — reflects a builder's approach to sports ownership rather than a trophy collector's. The returns, he insists, will follow the passion.
